routes.description: Establish that objective evaluative relations can be known through defeasible intellectual appearances, without requiring moral facts to figure in the best explanation of observations, and that practical reasoning cannot be fully grounded in antecedent desires or self-conception.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if moral appearances have prima facie justificatory force, the explanation-only restriction on evidence is not required, and objective evaluative facts are needed to account for at least some practical reasons or evident moral relations such as the badness of suffering.

motionBridge.description: Connect justified, undefeated moral appearances to knowledge of objective moral facts without making best-explanation evidence the exclusive path to justification.

centralBridges.description: Establish a defeasible entitlement to accept how matters intellectually appear unless a relevant defeater is supplied.
Show that explanatory inference depends on prior representational or rational entitlements and therefore cannot be the sole source of justified belief.
Show that desire strength, idealized desire, or self-conception cannot fully determine rational priority without independent evaluative facts.
Connect a priori access to objective natures or relations with the proposition that suffering is bad.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use nonmoral necessary relations to support a model of a priori knowledge that is not exhausted by linguistic synonymy or conceptual stipulation.
Account for cases in which evaluative judgment shapes emotion, desire, or conduct rather than merely projecting antecedent attitudes.

routes.description: Establish that objective morality would require desire-independent categorical reasons that do not fit practical deliberation, while moral appearances receive naturalistic explanations that do not require moral truths and therefore cannot justify moral knowledge.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if practical reasons must connect to an agent's values or deliberative perspective, objective morality requires reasons lacking that connection, and experiences support beliefs only through explanatory or causal relations that leave moral facts evidentially unnecessary.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of categorical moral reasons and the explanatory redundancy of moral facts to error theory and denial of justified moral knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Establish that practical reasons must derive normative purchase from an agent's desires, values, or deliberative perspective rather than from wholly external demands.
Show that objective morality requires desire-independent categorical reasons and that such reasons are not supplied by an internal account of practical rationality.
Require beliefs to gain evidential support through causal or best-explanation relations to experience rather than from the apparent propositional content alone.
Provide an explanation of moral appearances through psychological, emotional, social, or predictive processes that does not posit objective moral facts.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish an agent's deliberatively central commitments from momentarily forceful or alien desires so that internal reasons need not track motivational intensity.
Explain conceptual and a priori seemings through predictive refinement or relations among concepts without treating their apparent contents as foundational evidence.

sections.title: Objective Moral Facts and Categorical Reasons
sections.rationale: Covers the motion-level dispute over whether morality requires desire-independent categorical reasons and whether the nature of practical rationality supports or excludes objective moral facts.

sections.title: Appearances, Explanation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Covers the central epistemological clash over whether undefeated appearances provide prima facie justification or whether evidential support must instead arise through causal or best-explanation relations.

sections.title: Desire, Self-Conception, and Practical Reason
sections.rationale: Covers competing accounts of rational priority involving desire strength, idealized desire, deliberative identity, alienation, and the proposed need for independent evaluative standards.

sections.title: Moral Judgment, Emotion, and Motivation
sections.rationale: Covers whether moral judgments project antecedent attitudes or can independently organize emotion, desire, and conduct, including the implications of abandoning belief in moral facts.

sections.title: A Priori Knowledge, Concepts, and Objective Relations
sections.rationale: Covers whether mathematical, conceptual, and modal seemings are explained by conceptual learning or disclose objective natures and relations, including the proposed extension to suffering and badness.
